items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent environments that produce unanimous agreement, both in intended interactions that need coordination and in unintended emergent interactions. Consequently, understanding how LLMs with competing incentives reach consensus is crucial to better interpret and design LLM collectives. We introduce an evaluation, based on the Network Consensus game, to assess the mechanisms driving this process. Here, a network of agents must agree on one of two colours to receive a payoff, but agents are offered different payoffs for the agreed colour. We vary components such as communication access and network structure and assess six open-source models and one closed model (ChatGPT 5.6-sol). We find that open-source LLMs reach consensus less often than humans in comparable experiments and only if messages are communicated across the global network. ChatGPT 5.6-sol, however, is able to reach consensus with communication limited to its neighbours and with no communication ability. This is achieved through lower stubbornness and higher majority-following tendencies, and by providing more information about its neighbours' states in messages. However, situating agents in a highly clustered graph reduces consensus, regardless of these traits, demonstrating that both system design and individual model traits drive collective outcomes.
items.title: Drivers of LLM Consensus Formation Under Competing Incentives: A Simulation Study

items.summary: Background. Antireflux fundoplication failure — recurrent reflux, dysphagia, gas-bloat syndrome, secondary to a herniated, slipped, too-tight, disrupted, or twisted valve — remains common, and its endoscopic diagnosis lacks a common, standardized reporting language. Aim. To narratively review existing endoscopic instruments for postoperative antireflux valve assessment, the evidence on their interobserver reliability, and to position an original instrument — the Endoscopic Fundoplication Score (SEF) — within this landscape. Methods. Narrative review, with a targeted search in PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar (last search: 24 September 2026) using the terms “fundoplication,” “endoscopic grading,” “gastroesophageal valve,” “Hill classification,” “antireflux surgery outcome,” “interobserver reliability,” “wrap integrity,” and “hiatal hernia recurrence,” covering literature published between 1996 and 2026 in English or with an English abstract, supplemented by reference-list screening of identified articles. Results. Three major endoscopic instruments were identified — the Hill classification (1996), the Jobe system (2004), and the American Foregut Society (AFS) nomenclature (2025) — alongside a descriptive, non-scored taxonomy of failure types (herniated, slipped, tight, disrupted, twisted). The interobserver reliability studies [1,2] identified in this review for the postoperative setting report low agreement, and a retrospective comparison of endoscopy reports [3] documented major discrepancies between external endoscopists and operating surgeons. The AFS classification of esophagogastric junction integrity achieved substantial agreement on static images (κ=0.65) but only fair agreement under dynamic conditions (κ=0.371), and the postoperative AFS nomenclature has not yet been tested for interobserver reliability. The SEF score, an 11-item composite instrument (0–16 points) applied to a cohort of 178 patients, correlated in preliminary single-centre data with the Hill classification, Los Angeles (LA) esophagitis grade, and the Visick patient-satisfaction score (own data, manuscript submitted for publication), offering a numeric, quantifiable alternative to existing categorical systems. The SEF threshold of ≤10 points, defined in the same cohort, is exploratory. Conclusions. The field of postoperative endoscopic antireflux valve assessment remains fragmented, without an interobserver-reliable consensus standard. The SEF score partially addresses this gap through a numeric structure, with experience-based weights and an exploratory threshold, but requires formal interobserver reliability testing and multicenter validation against the surgical gold standard.
items.title: ENDOSCOPIC EVALUATION OF THE ANTIREFLUX VALVE AFTER FUNDOPLICATION: SYNTHESIS OF THE EVIDENCE AND PROPOSAL OF A FUNCTIONAL ENDOSCOPIC SCORE

items.summary: The capabilities of an agent swarm depend on both its individual members and how they coordinate. Yet existing multi-agent systems often train agents within fixed orchestration structures, separating the learning of individual capabilities from the organization of collective behavior. We introduce market-based post-training (MPT), a framework for jointly learning action policies and self-orchestration in decentralized agent swarms. Agents express their willingness to participate through bids, which determine who acts and how collective outcomes provide local training credit. Learning both action and bidding behavior allows individual capabilities and patterns of participation to adapt together without a central coordinating agent. We evaluate MPT on embodied crafting, robot navigation, and deep research. Results show gains over monolithic post-training and confirm that agent participation indeed evolves with learning. With the same post-trained action policies, learned self-orchestration outperforms alternative coordination strategies. Ablations show that both action and bidding benefit from learning, and that learned bids provide more effective action-training signals. Beyond the original training objectives, trained swarms adapt faster to related tasks and achieve better performance with larger populations at inference time. Larger populations also suffer smaller performance losses under agent dropout, demonstrating that learned self-orchestration supports reuse, scaling, and robustness in decentralized agent swarms. Code and trained models are available at https://github.com/Embodied-Minds-Lab/MPT.
items.title: Learning Self-Orchestration in Decentralized Agent Swarms

items.summary: Agents are increasingly interacting with other agents that act for different principals (people or organizations on whose behalf they work), such as a buyer's personal agent negotiating with an enterprise's seller agent. In such agent-to-agent (A2A) scenarios, each agent has its own environment and holds information and authority that the other cannot see. Moreover, the interests of each agent may be aligned (cooperative), partly aligned (mixed-motive), or opposed (competitive). Existing multi-agent system failure studies assume one orchestrator, shared workspace, or single principal. We ask how A2A systems fail when these assumptions are removed. We study more than 2,500 recorded runs of A2A systems built from different agent harnesses and models, spanning 488 scenarios across eight families (legal, CRM, security, commerce, etc.). From these traces, we derive $A^2$-Failures, a taxonomy of 20 A2A failure modes in four categories: (i) discovery and delegation, (ii) grounding and record consistency, (iii) verification, and (iv) conduct and fidelity. Three findings hold across every harness, model, and scenario studied: (1) discovery and interaction are driven by the phrasing of the task rather than the availability of peer agents; (2) no agent verifies a peer's factual claim on its own initiative, so an A2A system inherits the reliability of its least reliable participant unless the protocol or mechanism performs the check; and (3) the aggregate outcome score credits the agent completing the task while staying blind to the coordination, verification, and conduct failures beneath it, so A2A systems must be evaluated per agent, against each agent's own principal. We release the run logs behind the taxonomy at https://huggingface.co/datasets/a2a-salesforce/a2-failures.
items.title: Why Do Agent Teams Fail Across Boundaries? A Failure Taxonomy for Agent-to-Agent Systems with Private States

items.summary: AUTONOMOUS NANOROBOTIC NAVIGATION AND MISSION OBSERVABILITY AT THE LIMIT First-Generation Research Flagship 01 | NANO/MICRO ROBOTICS, POWER & MISSION ENDURANCE Feng Cheng-en (33) x Starli This research atlas asks a difficult engineering question: when low-Reynolds-number microfluidic flows, Brownian orientation noise, boundary adhesion, external field actuation and incomplete sensing all influence a micro/nanorobot, what would justify calling its behavior autonomous navigation rather than externally assisted motion? The volume treats navigation as an auditable, bounded mission instead of an attractive trajectory. It develops a five-layer program spanning stochastic hydrodynamics, instrument and actuation provenance, uncertainty-calibrated belief-state estimation, blinded microfluidic challenges and independent requalification. Thirty linked mathematical stations differentiate physical relations, information-theoretic functionals and proposed navigation utility measures, with assumptions, dimensions and possible falsifiers. Eighty-two research chapters each open with a core mathematical relation, followed by five independent single-page research sections. Two hundred detailed Research Gates describe decisive comparisons, confounding explanations, evidence requirements, failure conditions and successor handoff artifacts. Thirty-three provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos offer revisionable research prototypes rather than predetermined conclusions. The key comparator is an equal-budget experiment: fixed-field sequences, microscope-assisted manual control, externally tracked predictive control and candidate fused navigation are evaluated under matched total energy, information access, geometry, time, collision limits and recovery obligations. The manuscript emphasizes blind targets, flow reversal, sensor dropouts, wall adhesion, correlated observations, full-system power accounting, censored failures and post-mission retrieval. A mission arriving at its target but leaving an unrecovered device is not counted as a fully closed success. This work is a hypothesis-generating Research Atlas v1.0, not an experimental report or a validated medical technology. External magnetic, acoustic, optical and microscope infrastructure must be disclosed; no in-vivo or clinical competence is inferred from bench-top movement. Foundational DOI-linked literature provides context, not proof of the proposed integrated system. Every major claim is designed to be revised, rejected or reconstructed by a successor team using raw evidence and pre-registered falsification rules. items.summary: Multi-agent systems are increasingly used to solve coding tasks by coordinating agents that share code and plans. These agents are often optimized with reinforcement learning (RL) using automated evaluators, but bypassing evaluation can earn reward without producing a genuine solution. Prior work has largely treated reward hacking as a single-agent failure. In this work, we show that a reward-hacking strategy elicited in one agent can propagate to others and affect system coordination. Across four open-weight backbones, coding RL elicits and amplifies reward hacking in two settings: explicit mechanism descriptions in the system prompt and mid-training that models upstream exposure to facts about the coding environment. Using post-RL agents from the mid-training setting as sources, we observe propagation through code and shared memory, and across roles through natural-language plans. Even agents based on small open-weight models induce reward hacking in stronger closed-weight targets. On hard tasks, propagation can intensify along a transmission chain after the original source leaves as the code acquires more persuasive justifications. We also theoretically analyze conditions under which reward hacking amplifies, persists, or decays across agent interactions. Beyond propagation, reward hacking can bias task routing toward reward-hacking agents and survive candidate aggregation. As potential mitigations, we evaluate code review by the coder or a separate verifier, both of which reduce delivered hacks. Together, these results establish reward hacking as a transmissible strategy whose effects extend beyond the agent in which it first emerges.
items.title: Reward Hacking as a Transmissible Strategy in Multi-Agent Coding Systems

items.summary: We consider the three-dimensional Prandtl boundary layer equations near a smooth structured solution (u_s, K u_s) with ∂z K ≡ 0. Under a monotone-or-degenerate profile assumption on u_s(·), we prove local well-posedness, continuous dependence, and a priori estimates in the critical Sobolev space X^s = H^s_γ(r) × H^s_γ(q) × H^s_γ(∇{x,y} q), where r = u − u_s and q = v − K u. Our proof does not assume smallness of the data, monotonicity of ∂_z u_s, or Gevrey regularity. We also establish a nonlinear norm-inflation result showing that the raw H^s topology on q alone is insufficient, and we identify the minimal tangential derivative of q required. Several stress tests, counterexamples, and open problems are discussed.
items.title: Sobolev Well-Posedness for Three-Dimensional Prandtl Boundary Layers Near Proportional Structures in a Critical Transverse Space

items.summary: We investigate the rigidity of smooth stationary solutions to the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations in ℝⁿ with singularities along a linear subspace Σ ≅ ℝᵏ. Assuming the scale-invariant transverse bound ‖u(x)‖ ≤ C‖x′‖⁻¹, where x′ ∈ ℝᵐ represents the transverse coordinates and m = n − k is the codimension of the singularity, we prove that u ≡ 0 provided m ≥ 4 and 1 ≤ k < m. This result generalizes the recent theorem of Gui, Liu, Wang, and Xie (2026), which corresponds to the case k = 1 and n ≥ 5. Our proof relies on a quantitative local regularity theorem showing that the transverse bound implies the removability of the singularity along Σ. The argument combines weak extension across the subspace, approximate Green functions for the adjoint drift operator, a one-sided bound for the total head pressure, and a localized Frehse–Růžička weighted estimate followed by a finite Stokes–Morrey bootstrap. Furthermore, we establish the sharpness of the codimension threshold m ≥ 4 by constructing non-trivial counterexamples for m = 1, m = 2, and m = 3 via trivial extensions of Jeffery–Hamel and Landau solutions, together with a new explicit family of non-trivial solutions in the borderline case m = 1. Finally, we discuss the technical obstruction preventing the immediate removal of the condition k < m and propose a conditional rigidity result under additional integrability assumptions.
items.title: RIGIDITY OF STATIONARY NAVIER–STOKES SOLUTIONS WITH TRANSVERSE BOUNDS NEAR HIGHER-CODIMENSIONAL SINGULAR SUBSPACES

items.summary: As autonomous agents become widely deployed, coordinating access to shared computing resources and services will become increasingly important. Recent incidents have already revealed unplanned coordination between agents, highlighting the safety implications of these interactions. Yet prior studies of agent negotiation often use stylized games and simulated bargaining, leaving open how these behaviors develop during sustained, long-horizon tasks. We propose SCARCE (Shared Compute ARena for Coding agEnts), a framework in which agents solve sequences of coding tasks under individual deadlines while negotiating access to a shared execution resource. This negotiation determines when and for how long they can inspect programs, compile code, and run tests. We find that agents spontaneously develop informal institutions: persistent rules and commitments grounded in reputation, reciprocity, and precedent. These arrangements, which we call institutional behaviors, carry across tasks and influence resource allocation, with agents sometimes foregoing immediate advantages to honor earlier agreements. We develop a 21-category taxonomy of negotiation strategies and emergent norms and use it to analyze eight models and audit more than 1,500 trajectories across different environmental settings. Among the models tested, newer frontier models exhibit more institutional behaviors than older or lightweight models. Alongside cooperation, we observe exclusionary coalitions and rare divide-and-conquer strategies. SCARCE provides a controlled setting for proactively and systematically auditing how these relationships emerge, shape access to resources, and affect the safety and coordination of multi-agent systems.
items.title: SCARCE: Emergent Institutions in Long-Horizon Multi-Agent Coding Systems

items.summary: Safe multi-agent coordination typically assumes what real-world, deployed, resource-constrained robots cannot provide: continuous, perfect state sharing. Robust control strategies must be complemented with robust communication strategies to deliver resilient deployments. In this work, we propose a unified control/communication strategy that provides safe control to guarantee inter-agent safety under intermittent communication and demonstrate its effectiveness in a pursuit-evasion scenario. Each agent computes the reachable set of neighboring agents based on the last state information received, then solves for a safe control input based on control barrier functions to ensure agents avoid collision. We prove that inter-agent collision avoidance is guaranteed provided communication staleness remains bounded. As the reachable set inflates between state transmissions, each agent reasons about when to preemptively transmit its state information to neighboring agents based on novel metrics characterizing uncertainty risk and kinematic risk. We implement and simulate a variety of pursuit-evasion scenarios and show that preemptive communication reduces messages by 77.5% compared to periodic and event-triggered baselines with zero collisions.
items.title: Robust Multi-Agent Pursuit with Preemptive Communication via Reachability-Based Control Barrier Functions

items.summary: Scripts, dated analysis plans, run logs, and deal-level estimates for a study of 38,991 completed acquisitions by listed or delisted acquirers across 37 countries, rumored between 2007 and 2025. Version 2.1 accompanies a manuscript under double anonymized peer review; author identification is withheld during the review. It changes no script, log, plan, or data file of version 2.0: it updates the title of the manuscript and renumbers the exhibits in the index (NUMBERS.md) to those of the manuscript as submitted (Tables 1 to 6; Online Appendix S1 to S22). Licensed return series and deal and firm data cannot be redistributed and are documented rather than included (LICENSE_AND_DATA.md). Start with README.md.
items.title: Replication package: Do acquisitions change systematic risk? Evidence on beta from 38,991 deals in 37 countries over 19 years

items.summary: We provide a distributed online algorithm for multi-agent submodular coordination in bandit environments, i.e., environments whose evolution is unknown a priori and may even adapt to the agents' actions. We are motivated by multi-robot tasks such as target tracking, where the optimal actions change over time and the agents must track them rather than a single fixed optimum. To address such problems, we provide the Optimistic Distributed Online Greedy (O-DOG) algorithm, that leverages predictions about the environment's behavior and improves regret guarantees. The agents select actions simultaneously over arbitrary, possibly time-varying, network topologies, and each agent acts optimistically, i.e., leveraging predictions of its upcoming rewards, e.g., from forecasts of the targets' motion and of its neighbors' actions. We bound O-DOG's tracking regret in terms of the agents' prediction error and the bound never exceeds its prediction-free counterpart. Particularly, it is sublinear even when the optimal action changes at every time step, provided the predictions are accurate enough. We further quantify the suboptimality due to decentralization as a function of the network structure, and show that accurate predictions accelerate convergence. We validate O-DOG in simulated multi-robot target tracking.
items.title: Optimistic Distributed Submodular Coordination with Applications to Multi-Target Tracking with Multiple Robots

items.summary: Digital advertising is an important means for platforms to reach potential users and drive business growth. Advertising delivery is the core link between marketing objectives and actual returns. Existing methods have achieved partial automation in individual tasks such as bidding and budget allocation, but they still rely on human operators for overall coordination, making it difficult to support large-scale operations. They also often fail to achieve optimal performance, and individual experience remains difficult to turn into reusable operational capabilities. In addition, as advertising markets change, advertising delivery systems need timely strategy updates to remain effective in dynamic markets. To automate the entire advertising operations process and improve adaptability to market changes, we propose AdCoEvo, a co-evolving multi-agent advertising delivery system. Specifically, the system connects delivery decisions across different timescales and operational granularities through role specialization. Diagnostic results guide account planning and strategy adjustment in the next period. The multi-agent system updates its model parameters based on actual delivery outcomes and continually improves delivery strategies through mutual feedback among planning, adjustment, and diagnosis, thereby achieving co-evolution. Experiments show that, relative to the rule-based operational baseline (Rule), AdCoEvo increases advertiser value by 14.02% while reducing cost per acquisition by 7.07%. Compared with a multi-agent system with fixed parameters, AdCoEvo increases advertiser value by 3.96% and reduces cost per acquisition by 1.24%, indicating that co-evolution can yield greater delivery returns.
items.title: AdCoEvo: A Co-Evolving Multi-Agent Advertising Delivery System

items.summary: When robots are deployed in the real-world, they must interact with other agents and accomplish their own goals while adhering to legal constraints. These potentially conflicting objectives are often only partially prioritized, making scalarized objectives or fully specified hierarchies unsuitable. We present a framework for multi-agent motion planning under legal requirements based on games with partially ordered preferences (posetal games). Scenario-independent legal guidelines order abstract legal concerns, from which we automatically derive agent preferences and a legal game for any concrete scenario. Agents may refine their legal preferences with private objectives, and regulators may refine the guideline as laws evolve. We prove that such customizations can only remove equilibria and thus preserve legality. To coordinate agents without explicitly communicating private preferences, we introduce belief play, which provably recovers the true equilibria from conservative local games, and a distributed iterative best-response protocol requiring less information. We apply the framework to maritime navigation, systematically lifting pairwise traffic rules to multi-vessel encounters. On seven encounters with up to four vessels, every rule violation of the committed equilibria is certified as forced by the legal hierarchy or unsatisfiable, and defectors are identified from public information in all tested cases. These results indicate that guideline-based posetal games offer an auditable route from partially specified laws to multi-agent motion planning.
items.title: Auditable and Deployable Multi-Agent Motion Planning via Posetal Games from Legal Guidelines

items.summary: Scripts, dated analysis plans, run logs, and deal-level estimates for a study of 38,991 completed acquisitions by listed or delisted acquirers across 37 countries, rumored between 2007 and 2025. Version 2.1 accompanies a manuscript under double anonymized peer review; author identification is withheld during the review. It changes no script, log, plan, or data file of version 2.0: it updates the title of the manuscript and renumbers the exhibits in the index (NUMBERS.md) to those of the manuscript as submitted (Tables 1 to 6; Online Appendix S1 to S22). items.title: Replication package: Do acquisitions change systematic risk? Evidence on beta from 38,991 deals in 37 countries over 19 years

items.summary: Multi-agent LLM systems rely on generative models for expert execution, workflow planning, and artifact review. Yet many coordination operations require only bounded decisions, such as selecting the next expert or judging artifact quality. Profiling three representative MAS frameworks, we find that routing and review account for 31.7-43.5% of generative-LLM tokens. However, replacing these operations with low-cost decision models introduces two interface gaps: generative planners produce execution plans and handoff instructions (planning gap), while reviewers provide actionable feedback for repairing flawed artifacts (review gap), which bounded decisions alone cannot provide. We introduce Jev-LiteMAS, a multi-agent framework that bridges both gaps by combining a lightweight decision model (Jev) with generative execution and feedback. To address the planning gap, Jev selects experts dynamically from the task and prior expert outputs, using accumulated context to ground subsequent execution without a pre-generated trajectory. To address the review gap, Jev screens intermediate artifacts against task criteria: passing artifacts proceed directly, whereas flagged ones undergo LLM re-review for acceptance or corrective feedback. Across four benchmarks and two backbones, Jev-LiteMAS reduces generative-LLM tokens by 12.7-54.6% over LAS, maintaining accuracy within 1.34 percentage points and lowering latency in seven of eight settings. Grounding routing in substantive expert outputs prevents up to 18.0 points in accuracy loss.
items.title: Jev-LiteMAS: Separating Decisions from Generation in Multi-Agent Workflows

items.summary: Cooperative driving at mixed-traffic unsignalized intersections is challenged by imperfect vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication, human-driven vehicle (HV) intentions that cannot be directly communicated, and the potential incompatibility of independently generated crossing decisions. This paper proposes State-Intent-Aware Graph Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Cooperative Driving under Imperfect V2X (SIGN-MAPPO) to address these challenges through three coordinated mechanisms. Each decision-eligible connected and automated vehicle (CAV) first reconstructs a receiver-specific traffic graph from its ego state and the peer-state records available to it, from which a shared graph-attention policy generates a raw Stop/Go intention augmented with predicted HV-intent features. CAV intentions are then exchanged through timestamped vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) messages, and a local conflict-aware arbitration layer converts each CAV's intention into a safe executable action despite potentially inconsistent peer information. In the principal Simulation of Urban MObility (SUMO) evaluation, SIGN-MAPPO achieves a 97.53% completion rate, a 0.10% collision rate, and a mean intersection traversal time of 35.28 s. Ablation studies further confirm the complementary contributions of HV-intent prediction and CAV-intent exchange to this performance. The trained policy also remains robust under the evaluated communication-delay and packet-loss ranges, and cross-scenario tests show complete traffic clearance across the tested settings, though safety margins narrow under compound unpredictable HV behavior.
items.title: SIGN-MAPPO: State-Intent-Aware Graph Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Cooperative Driving under Imperfect V2X

items.summary: Multi-agent path finding (MAPF) solvers are evaluated on the schedules they produce, not on how well those schedules can be executed. Specifically, continuous-time optimal solvers can achieve even lower cost than their discrete counterparts by scheduling agents with near-zero temporal/spatial separation, and by exploiting graphs with higher connectedness; however, such schedules may prove hard to execute under a realistic controller. We integrate AOC-CBS, an anytime-optimal continuous-time MAPF solver, into a fleet coordination framework in which each agent tracks its timed path using model predictive control, and we evaluate the resulting system on congested MovingAI benchmark instances with 21 to 40 agents. Without intervention, only a fraction of the instances complete execution. We then apply T-robustness by adding a time-margin, i.e., a minimum temporal gap between agents at shared locations, as well as spatial inflation of the agent footprint. Increasing either margin raises execution success, for a relatively small increase in the schedule's sum-of-costs; it also improves how closely agents adhere to the schedule: when tracking each agent's position throughout execution and comparing it against the position it should occupy according to the schedule, the mean discrepancy falls significantly as the margin increases. In general, the two margins have different effects; temporal margin decreases deviation, giving the controller room to stay on schedule. Spatial margin affects deviation less and instead increases the clearance between agents, so that the same deviation no longer leads to a blocking stall. They are nonetheless substitutes rather than complements: spatial inflation is almost free in schedule cost, but its effect on execution success is small and does not compound with a temporal margin already in place.
items.title: The Cost of Executability: Temporal Margins for Continuous-Time Multi-Agent Path Finding under Closed-Loop Control

items.summary: The Mathematics of 3D Printing Slicing: STL Geometry, Ray-Casting & Toolpaths is an open-access engineering monograph and interactive instructional module published by the Prep4Uni.Online OER Initiative . This work provides an analytical, undergraduate/postgraduate-level treatment of the computational geometry foundations required to translate three-dimensional surface meshes into layer-by-layer machine toolpaths. Aligned with international accreditation standards—specifically the Washington Accord (WA1–WA5) and EUR-ACE First/Second Cycle frameworks—this publication establishes the mathematical proofs, vector algorithms, and point-in-polygon logic governing modern additive manufacturing slicing software. Core Mathematical & Computational Themes: STL Topology & Facet Representation: Analysis of unstructured triangulated surface meshes, outward unit normal vectors (\(\mathbf{n}\)), vertex coordinate systems, and planar boundary extraction. Parametric Facet-Plane Intersection: Step-by-step vector linear interpolation for deriving the intersection segment \(S_k\) formed by cutting planes at \(z = z_k\), addressing non-manifold edges, vertex touching, and numerical epsilon shifts. Jordan Curve Theorem & Parity Logic: Formal implementation of the 2D Ray-Casting algorithm and Even-Odd Parity test for robust interior, exterior, and internal void classification across arbitrary closed slices. Toolpath Trajectory Generation: Comparative kinematics and geometry between continuous concentric perimeter offset loops and 45° zigzag parallel hatch raster patterns. Formative Assessment Suite: A three-tier verification suite comprising 8 foundational concepts, 7 real-world slicer failure debugging scenarios, and 6 step-by-step quantitative engineering worked examples. Note: The full interactive web edition—featuring client-side HTML5 simulation canvas engines, dynamic parameter sliders, and real-time slice projection mathematics—is accessible at: https://prep4uni.online/stem/physical-technologies/industrial-and-manufacturing-technologies/additive-manufacturing-3d-printing/mathematics-of-slicing/
items.title: The Mathematics of 3D Printing Slicing: STL Geometry, Ray-Casting & Toolpaths

items.summary: Centralized orchestration provides comprehensive multi-agent coordination but creates bottlenecks in scalability, adaptability, and collective performance. Decentralized approaches alleviate these bottlenecks by distributing coordination across agents, yet often leave responsibility for delegated dependencies and failure recovery unclear. To address this gap, we propose RCM, a responsibility-centered coordination mechanism that leverages commitments to couple task delegation with explicit responsibilities of the involved parties. Through recursive delegation, agents retain their upstream responsibilities while locally orchestrating downstream commitments, thereby preserving accountability across delegation chains, creating a network of local orchestration. We operationalize this mechanism locally through responsibility-constrained decision-making and a responsibility-oriented communication protocol (RCP), enabling agents to autonomously establish, manage, and terminate commitments. As agents act in parallel, their local actions continuously evolve the commitment graph, allowing global coordination to emerge and adapt toward a shared mission without centralized control. Experiments across reasoning, coding, and executable agent environments demonstrate that RCM outperforms strong centralized and decentralized coordination baselines by up to 18.7 points in task performance and 10.2 points in Responsibility, while improving failure and harm detection without task-specific training.
items.title: A Responsibility-Centered Coordination Mechanism for Decentralized Multi-Agent Systems

items.summary: Background. Antireflux fundoplication failure — recurrent reflux, dysphagia, gas-bloat syndrome, secondary to a herniated, slipped, too-tight, disrupted, or twisted valve — remains common, and its endoscopic diagnosis lacks a common, standardized reporting language. Aim. To narratively review existing endoscopic instruments for postoperative antireflux valve assessment, the evidence on their interobserver reliability, and to position an original instrument — the Endoscopic Fundoplication Score (SEF) — within this landscape. Methods. Narrative review, with a targeted search in PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar (last search: 24 September 2026) using the terms “fundoplication,” “endoscopic grading,” “gastroesophageal valve,” “Hill classification,” “antireflux surgery outcome,” “interobserver reliability,” “wrap integrity,” and “hiatal hernia recurrence,” covering literature published between 1996 and 2026 in English or with an English abstract, supplemented by reference-list screening of identified articles. Results. Three major endoscopic instruments were identified — the Hill classification (1996), the Jobe system (2004), and the American Foregut Society (AFS) nomenclature (2025) — alongside a descriptive, non-scored taxonomy of failure types (herniated, slipped, tight, disrupted, twisted). The interobserver reliability studies [1,2] identified in this review for the postoperative setting report low agreement, and a retrospective comparison of endoscopy reports [3] documented major discrepancies between external endoscopists and operating surgeons. The AFS classification of esophagogastric junction integrity achieved substantial agreement on static images (κ=0.65) but only fair agreement under dynamic conditions (κ=0.371), and the postoperative AFS nomenclature has not yet been tested for interobserver reliability. The SEF score, an 11-item composite instrument (0–16 points) applied to a cohort of 178 patients, correlated in preliminary single-centre data with the Hill classification, Los Angeles (LA) esophagitis grade, and the Visick patient-satisfaction score (own data, manuscript submitted for publication), offering a numeric, quantifiable alternative to existing categorical systems. The SEF threshold of ≤10 points, defined in the same cohort, is exploratory. Conclusions. The field of postoperative endoscopic antireflux valve assessment remains fragmented, without an interobserver-reliable consensus standard. The SEF score partially addresses this gap through a numeric structure, with experience-based weights and an exploratory threshold, but requires formal interobserver reliability testing and multicenter validation against the surgical gold standard.
items.title: ENDOSCOPIC EVALUATION OF THE ANTIREFLUX VALVE AFTER FUNDOPLICATION: SYNTHESIS OF THE EVIDENCE AND PROPOSAL OF A FUNCTIONAL ENDOSCOPIC SCORE

items.summary: Long-horizon embodied agents must maintain task-relevant information, coordinate heterogeneous robots, and adapt their decisions as execution unfolds. Existing benchmarks investigate dynamic task execution and embodied multi-agent coordination, but provide limited evaluation of their intersection. We introduce MAGMA-Bench, an architecture-agnostic benchmark for persistent task reasoning in dynamic multi-robot environments. MAGMA-Bench evaluates agents across increasing task horizons and controlled online perturbations, including execution failures, task interruptions, and mission updates, with scenarios requiring coordination across robots with heterogeneous capabilities. It uses a structured skill-level interface to separate task-level reasoning from perception and low-level control. We evaluate locally deployable open-weight planners, multi-agent state-tracking strategies, and frontier models. Even the strongest evaluated models fail on a substantial fraction of clean episodes, and their success rates decrease further under online perturbations. Supervised adaptation greatly improves a small model, but performance remains substantially lower on longer and multi-robot missions. We release the benchmark, 261,646 task-level training examples, and an architecture-agnostic expert-trace generation pipeline.
items.title: MAGMA-Bench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Embodied Agents under Dynamic Tasks and Execution Failures

items.summary: EHR2Trace converts local hospital EHR extracts (delimited text and spreadsheets) into OMOP CDM 5.4 and MEDS. The two targets are derived independently from a single canonical layer rather than one from the other, every published row carries a link back to the source rows it came from, and fifty-five checks encode the properties a conversion must satisfy before it can be used as training data, including the leakage failures that are invisible to schema validation. Where the data does not answer a question, the converter blocks and says so instead of substituting a default. Companion paper: EHR2Trace: Auditable EHR Data Infrastructure for Patient World Models and Clinical Agents (arXiv:2609.38193).
items.title: EHR2Trace: a deterministic converter from local EHR exports to OMOP CDM 5.4 and MEDS, with row-level lineage

items.summary: Medical prescribing errors for multimorbid patients, who require complex drug regimens, are a major patient safety concern. These errors often stem from fragmented decision-making across medical specialties, a critical coordination failure that leads to adverse drug events and rehospitalizations. To address this coordination challenge, we introduce PRISMATIC, a multi-agent architecture where specialized agents, each representing a workflow role, collaboratively generate and refine treatment plans. Operating on a blackboard architecture, the system first structures patient information from clinical notes, then iteratively develops safe, rational, and interpretable drug regimens. The agents' collaboration is governed by two novel adaptive coordination mechanisms: (1) Dynamic Self-Updating Weight Adjustment (DSWA), a long-term mechanism that adjusts the influence weights of agents based on historical case outcomes, enabling the system to adapt and trust more reliable specialists over time. (2) Discrepancy Feedback Precise Calibration (DFPC), a short-term mechanism where agents provide iterative feedback to resolve disagreements and eliminate prescription conflicts for the current patient. Experiments on patient records from the MIMIC-IV database show that PRISMATIC significantly reduces drug conflicts, improves prescription coverage, and enhances treatment consistency compared to strong LLM baselines. Our work demonstrates that structuring clinical co-treatment as a multi-agent coordination problem offers a promising path toward safer and more coherent multidisease management.
items.title: PRISMATIC : Prescription Risk Inspection System for Multi-Agent Treatment Interaction in Clinical Decision-Making

items.summary: Long-horizon multi-agent collaboration requires memory that preserves both successful actions and the coordination structure underlying them. Existing memory systems support information sharing or procedural reuse, but often leave the evolution of shared procedures disconnected from the task dependencies and execution states of collaborating agents. This coupling also limits the direct transfer of procedural memory designed for individual agents to team settings. We propose Self-Evolving Procedural Memory (SEPM), a framework that uses task dependency graphs as a common representation for online coordination and procedural memory evolution. During execution, a lightweight shared blackboard records structured evidence alongside task dependencies, supporting the detection of goal, plan, and world-state divergence and evidence-based realignment. After execution, verified actions and dependencies are distilled into reusable procedures, while recurring failures inform warnings and constraints. The shared procedure pool evolves through creation, refinement, specialization, and retirement, guided by success and cost utility and constrained by evidence and safety requirements. Together, these mechanisms preserve the collaborative structure and applicability conditions needed to reuse experience across tasks. Evaluations on ALFWorld, WebArena, and OfficeBench under AutoGen and DyLAN show that SEPM achieves the highest task scores among the compared methods in all six benchmark settings. Under AutoGen, it improves task scores over the no-added-memory baseline by 29.85, 25.86, and 13.00 percentage points, respectively. The codebase is available at https://github.com/cookieApril/SEPM.
items.title: SEPM: Self-Evolving Procedural Memory Grounded in Task Graphs for Multi-Agent Collaboration

items.summary: This paper studies parameter families of finite exponential sums in which two tie endpoints of a near-maximum level set approach at the critical rate δ_r ≍ qr^{-1/2}. The endpoint separation, half-bowl width, and competitor-kernel decay length then coincide. The cluster trio is rigid: its three exponents are determined by the level and endpoint positions, while coefficient ratios and other competitors require separate control. In a realized family, six rescaled kernels carry the interaction through one microscopic phase. Under explicit kernel-convergence hypotheses, the second-order term has a joint limit given by the excess sublevel length of a limiting profile, decomposed into a separated-endpoint sum and an interaction term. For an explicit four-term family, the hypotheses are verified with uniform explicit constants for every admissible phase lock. Two families have identical spectra and corresponding coefficient moduli at every radius but different critical limits. Along an unlocked calibration, phase dependence yields non-existence of the critical limit for specified parameters; certified intervals quantify the gap, and failure persists on an open parameter set. For a positive zero-lock family, upper and lower bounds describe the excluded shared arc. Full exclusion never occurs, and nonempty exclusion requires an additional parameter condition. The formal endpoint-anchored cap cannot be realized by a family satisfying the cluster hypotheses. High-precision numerical measurements on actual exponential sums compare with the profiles and exhibit phase dependence.
items.title: Critical-Scale Clustering and the Breakdown of Universality for Near-Maximum Phase Measures of Exponential Sums

items.summary: Multi-agent collaboration has emerged as a critical paradigm for tackling complex, long-horizon tasks; however, while coordination protocols continue to advance, systemic failures at the inter-agent collaboration interface remain a pervasive bottleneck. In collaborative workflows, systems frequently suffer from \emph{broken handoffs}---where critical task context is omitted, misrouted, or ignored despite each agent emitting locally plausible responses. To address this challenge, we present \method, a verifiable runtime control framework that treats handoff repair as selective intervention over explicit dependency graphs. Central to \method is an integrated fault-attribution and calibration pipeline, \dataset, which decouples execution dependencies and injects counterfactual handoff perturbations to provide empirical supervision for runtime intervention. Leveraging this diagnostic foundation, \method dynamically compiles observable interaction traces into a provenance graph to pinpoint unresolved dependencies, without accessing private agent states. It then evaluates candidate repairs through an empirical gate that weighs expected gains against disruption risks, and executes repairs only when formal local postconditions hold. Extensive evaluations across demanding benchmarks demonstrate that \method boosts task success by up to 12.3 absolute percentage points on SILO-BENCH and 11.1 on TeamBench. Across both backbones, \method maintains strict cost-effectiveness, adding as little as 2.0\% marginal token overhead. Furthermore, on 562 handoff-relevant traces from the MAST benchmark, \method achieves 69.8\% F1 in a single pass, establishing a reliable operational boundary for verifiable coordination repair.
items.title: BRIDGE: Selective Boundary Repair with Dependency Graph Evidence in Multi-Agent Systems

items.summary: This paper studies parameter families of finite exponential sums in which two tie endpoints of a near-maximum level set approach at the critical rate δ_r ≍ qr^{-1/2}. The endpoint separation, half-bowl width, and competitor-kernel decay length then coincide. The cluster trio is rigid: its three exponents are determined by the level and endpoint positions, while coefficient ratios and other competitors require separate control. In a realized family, six rescaled kernels carry the interaction through one microscopic phase. Under explicit kernel-convergence hypotheses, the second-order term has a joint limit given by the excess sublevel length of a limiting profile, decomposed into a separated-endpoint sum and an interaction term. For an explicit four-term family, the hypotheses are verified with uniform explicit constants for every admissible phase lock. Two families have identical spectra and corresponding coefficient moduli at every radius but different critical limits. Along an unlocked calibration, phase dependence yields non-existence of the critical limit for specified parameters; certified intervals quantify the gap, and failure persists on an open parameter set. For a positive zero-lock family, upper and lower bounds describe the excluded shared arc. Full exclusion never occurs, and nonempty exclusion requires an additional parameter condition. The formal endpoint-anchored cap cannot be realized by a family satisfying the cluster hypotheses. High-precision numerical measurements on actual exponential sums compare with the profiles and exhibit phase dependence.
items.title: Critical-Scale Clustering and the Breakdown of Universality for Near-Maximum Phase Measures of Exponential Sums

items.summary: Multi-agent systems promise a new axis for scaling inference: rather than having one agent think longer or sample more attempts, a task is split across many agents that work in parallel and coordinate. However, in practice, more agents can easily produce duplicate work, coordination failures, and higher costs. We therefore formulate team design as a compute allocation problem: starting from a solo agent, where should additional inference compute go to reach the reward-cost Pareto frontier? We build a minimal multi-agent harness from the ground up and trace this frontier by varying, one at a time, the workflow stage at which a lead delegates to its workers (planning, implementation, or verification), the models that form the team, and the number of workers. On ProgramBench, teams outperform solo agents but cost three to seven times as much. With the right compute allocation, however, a heterogeneous 17-agent team comes within 1.4 points of a strong homogeneous 5-agent team at 70% lower cost. This efficiency stems from three findings. First, planning is the most valuable use of workers: in a homogeneous team whose lead decides how many workers to spawn, a lead that delegates only planning to its workers, and then implements and verifies the code itself, matches the reward of a lead that delegates to workers throughout planning, implementation, and verification, at half the cost. Second, cheap models pay off as planners but not as implementers: a strong lead with cheap planners recovers 47.5% of the reward gain of an all-strong team for only 13.9% of its additional cost, whereas cheap implementers lower reward. Third, planners keep improving reward as the team grows, whereas implementers and verifiers plateau beyond four workers. Together, our results offer a guide to spending an agent budget where it counts, given the task, cost, and latency constraints a user has.
items.title: Scaling Inference-Time Compute with Teams of Coding Agents

items.summary: The Mathematics of 3D Printing Slicing: STL Geometry, Ray-Casting & Toolpaths is an open-access engineering monograph and interactive instructional module published by the Prep4Uni.Online OER Initiative . This work provides an analytical, undergraduate/postgraduate-level treatment of the computational geometry foundations required to translate three-dimensional surface meshes into layer-by-layer machine toolpaths. Aligned with international accreditation standards—specifically the Washington Accord (WA1–WA5) and EUR-ACE First/Second Cycle frameworks—this publication establishes the mathematical proofs, vector algorithms, and point-in-polygon logic governing modern additive manufacturing slicing software. Core Mathematical & Computational Themes: STL Topology & Facet Representation: Analysis of unstructured triangulated surface meshes, outward unit normal vectors (\(\mathbf{n}\)), vertex coordinate systems, and planar boundary extraction. Parametric Facet-Plane Intersection: Step-by-step vector linear interpolation for deriving the intersection segment \(S_k\) formed by cutting planes at \(z = z_k\), addressing non-manifold edges, vertex touching, and numerical epsilon shifts. Jordan Curve Theorem & Parity Logic: Formal implementation of the 2D Ray-Casting algorithm and Even-Odd Parity test for robust interior, exterior, and internal void classification across arbitrary closed slices. Toolpath Trajectory Generation: Comparative kinematics and geometry between continuous concentric perimeter offset loops and 45° zigzag parallel hatch raster patterns. Formative Assessment Suite: A three-tier verification suite comprising 8 foundational concepts, 7 real-world slicer failure debugging scenarios, and 6 step-by-step quantitative engineering worked examples. Note: The full interactive web edition—featuring client-side HTML5 simulation canvas engines, dynamic parameter sliders, and real-time slice projection mathematics—is accessible at: https://prep4uni.online/stem/physical-technologies/industrial-and-manufacturing-technologies/additive-manufacturing-3d-printing/mathematics-of-slicing/

items.summary: Recent advances in deep learning have significantly improved underwater acoustic vessel recognition. However, existing publicly available datasets are typically limited in scale, hindering large-scale representation learning and downstream task evaluation. To address this limitation, we introduce ONCship, a large-scale underwater acoustic dataset comprising 4521 hours of curated recordings from Ocean Networks Canada (ONC) hydrophones and Automatic Identification System (AIS) data. We evaluate the proposed dataset across three tasks: self-supervised representation learning, vessel-type classification, and MMSI-Level Vessel Classification. Experiments on DeepShip and ShipsEar demonstrate the effectiveness of ONCship for acoustic representation learning, with joint pre-training on ONCship and AudioSet achieving a classification accuracy of 62.45% on DeepShip through linear probing. Furthermore, incorporating ONCship as auxiliary training data improves downstream vessel-type classification performance. Beyond conventional vessel-type classification, we further investigate MMSI-Level Vessel Classification, treating each vessel as a distinct identity. Experimental results show that models fine-tuned with different loss functions achieve Top-1 accuracies exceeding 53% and Top-5 accuracies approaching 69%, demonstrating the feasibility of distinguishing individual vessels through MMSI-Level Vessel Classification. Overall, ONCship provides a valuable resource for underwater acoustic representation learning and vessel recognition, while its rich vessel-level metadata enables further exploration of MMSI-Level Vessel Classification.
items.title: ONCship: A Large-Scale Underwater Acoustic Corpus for Ship Recognition

items.summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a Structured PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23431625 . Does the introduction explain the objective of the research presented in the preprint? Yes The introduction clearly explains the research objectives. It states that the study aims to replicate the quantitative analysis of Krause, Krause, and Bränfors (2018), assess the reproducibility of their findings, and examine potential limitations concerning statistical power and model specification. Are the methods well-suited for this research? Somewhat appropriate The replication approach is suitable for the research, as the authors reproduce the original Cox proportional hazards models and robustness tests. However, the methodological assessment has some gaps. In particular, the power analysis reports values of 0.44 and 0.99 without providing the formula, software procedure, or sufficient calculation details to allow readers to reproduce the estimates. The choice of 42 events in Table 6 also needs clarification, given that Table 5 reports 54 events overall. Additionally, the differences between the original and reproduced sample sizes remain unexplained. These issues weaken the transparency and reproducibility of the analysis. Are the conclusions supported by the data? Somewhat supported The main conclusion is that the original findings can be reproduced, which is supported by the reported results. The authors also reasonably identify the small number of female-signatory agreements and the limitations of drawing causal conclusions from the observed association. However, the claim that the analysis has low statistical power relies on a calculation for which the formula and detailed procedure are not provided (Table 6). The differences between the original and reproduced sample sizes also remain unexplained. These limitations make some aspects of the interpretation less conclusive than they could be. Are the data presentations, including visualizations, well-suited to represent the data? Somewhat appropriate and clear The survival analysis and regression tables are suitable for presenting the findings. However, some numerical inconsistencies in the descriptive statistics and differences in sample sizes across the original and reproduced models need clarification to ensure the results are presented accurately. For instance, Table 3 presents: three major statistical flaws: 1: Conflict Intensity row, where Female Signatories = 1: has SD of 1.2 while the Max is 0.45, which is statistically incorrect. Similarly, (2) Democracy row where Female Signatories = 1, has Mean 0.92 < Min 1. And lastly, on page 5, UN peacekeeping is written as a binary number, however, in Table 3, the binary UN Peacekeeping has Max > 1. All these minor inconsistencies require clarification. How clearly do the authors discuss, explain, and interpret their findings and potential next steps for the research? Very clearly The authors explain their findings, acknowledge the limitations of the small number of agreements with female signatories, and discuss the implications for causal interpretation.
